content: A muscle spasm is defined as a sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle, a group of muscles, a hollow organ, or an orifice. This contraction may sometimes be accompanied by a sudden onset of pain. However, in most cases, it is harmless and resolves on its own within a few minutes. Spasmodic muscle contractions can also occur as a result of various medical conditions, including dystonias, which are neurological disorders characterized by involuntary muscle contractions. In a broader sense, the term spasm can also refer to a temporary surge of energy, activity, or emotion. In certain cases, spasms can affect hollow organs, such as the bile duct. A common feature of colic, which involves spasms in hollow organs, is the sensation of needing to move around to alleviate discomfort. Severe colic pain may lead to associated symptoms such as nausea or vomiting. When spasms occur in a series or become persistent, the condition is referred to as spasmism. In extreme cases, spasms can cause muscle contractions that are significantly more forceful than what the individual could voluntarily produce under normal circumstances. Such intense contractions may result in injuries, including torn tendons or ligaments. There is also a hypothesis that hysterical strength, a phenomenon where individuals exhibit extraordinary physical strength during extreme situations, may be a type of spasm triggered by the brain under conditions of intense stress or danger.
